records.name: Saint Lucia
records.summary_text: Saint Lucia demands real caution. The Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court struck down sodomy/gross-indecency laws in July 2025 (Randall Theodule v AG) — the region's most recent decriminalisation, welcomed by the IACHR. Saint Lucia has a relatively organised community (ECADE, United and Strong) and hosts Pride. No LGR.

records.name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
records.summary_text: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines demands real caution — the Eastern Caribbean outlier: its High Court UPHELD the buggery laws in 2024 (unlike its neighbours), so criminalisation (10 years) remains formally in force. Enforcement is rare, but the legal floor and judicial hostility distinguish it from the decriminalised neighbours.

records.name: Grenada
records.summary_text: Grenada demands real caution. The buggery law (10 years) remains on the books (no successful court challenge yet), though unenforced; no LGR; small community; tourist areas insulated.

records.name: Bahamas
records.summary_text: The Bahamas demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 1991; tourism-dependent economy with extensive international exposure; no LGR; documented social hostility but no criminalisation and no police-targeting pattern.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in the Bahamas

records.name: Haiti
records.summary_text:
Haiti is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but the national government has effectively collapsed: gangs control most of the capital (Port-au-Prince), the police are outgunned, and mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition, no protection infrastructure, and no functioning judiciary.

The trans-specific risk is inseparable from the generalised collapse — outing in gang-controlled areas can be lethal. A 2018 official US State Department report described attitudes as hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public
